nameStory: The corn snake gets its name from the distinctive checkerboard pattern on its belly that resembles kernels of Indian corn (maize). Some say it's also called this because it's often found in cornfields and grain storage areas, where it hunts the mice and rats that come to feast on stored crops.
description: The corn snake is a beautiful, slender constrictor that's one of North America's most colorful serpents. These medium-sized snakes typically grow 2-4 feet long and sport vibrant orange or red bodies decorated with bold red or maroon blotches outlined in black. Their smooth, glossy scales give them an almost polished appearance, and their slender build makes them excellent climbers. Though they look similar to venomous copperheads, corn snakes are completely harmless to humans.

idTips.label: Pattern
idTips.description: Large, square-shaped red or maroon blotches with black borders run down an orange or red background, creating a striking checkerboard effect on the belly

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Narrow, elongated head that's only slightly wider than the neck, with round pupils and a pointed snout - quite different from a viper's triangular head

idTips.label: Scales
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy scales that feel like polished leather when touched, creating an almost silky texture unlike the rougher scales of many other snakes

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized snake typically 2-4 feet long with a slender, graceful build that feels surprisingly light and delicate when handled

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Excellent climber that often freezes motionless when spotted, then may vibrate its tail in leaves (creating a rattling sound) before fleeing

habitat: Corn snakes are extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation, as they naturally occur much further south. If encountered, they would likely be escaped pets rather than wild natives, possibly found near human settlements, old barns, or areas with abundant rodents.

seasonality.spring: Active after emerging from winter hiding spots, often seen basking in sunny areas during warm afternoons as they prepare for breeding season.
seasonality.summer: Most active during summer months, hunting primarily at dawn and dusk when temperatures are moderate and prey is active.
seasonality.fall: Feeding heavily in preparation for winter dormancy, may be found near grain storage areas following rodent activity.
seasonality.winter: Dormant in protected locations like rock crevices, old foundations, or deep leaf litter, rarely seen during cold months.

funFact: Corn snakes are such accomplished escape artists that herpetologists joke they can slip through any gap wider than their skull - and they can actually dislocate their jaw joints to squeeze through impossibly tight spaces, making them the Houdinis of the snake world.
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for the venomous copperhead, but corn snakes have a much more slender build, narrower head, round pupils, and distinctive black-bordered blotches rather than the copperhead's hourglass-shaped bands. Remember: 'Square blotches safe, hourglass dangerous.'
contextualKnowledge: Any corn snake found in New England is almost certainly an escaped or released pet, as this species doesn't naturally occur this far north. The pet trade has made corn snakes one of the most commonly kept reptiles due to their docile nature and beautiful colors.
compareHints: Unlike its close relative the Eastern Ratsnake (the only other Pantherophis species in New England), corn snakes are much more colorful with distinct red and orange hues rather than dark gray or black. Eastern Ratsnakes are also significantly larger, reaching 6+ feet, and have a more robust build with less defined pattern markings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The eastern ratsnake is much larger and darker than its relative the red cornsnake, which has an orange or reddish base color with distinct red blotches outlined in black.
